content: Selenium is an essential trace element that plays a critical role in human biology. It is a key component of various selenoproteins, including glutathione peroxidase, which is involved in protecting cells from oxidative damage. Selenium also contributes to the proper functioning of the immune system. In newborns, blood selenium levels are lower than those of their mothers, and these levels are even further reduced in preterm infants. Studies in experimental animals suggest that low selenium levels may increase the risk of oxidative lung disease. In very preterm infants, low selenium concentrations have been linked to a higher likelihood of developing chronic neonatal lung disease and retinopathy of prematurity. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of selenium supplementation in preterm or very low birth weight (VLBW) infants. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase, covering studies up to May 2003. Additional sources, such as reference lists of recent trials and abstracts from the Society for Pediatric Research (from 1990 onward), were also reviewed. The search was later updated in November 2010. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared selenium supplementation, administered either parenterally or enterally, with placebo or no supplementation in preterm or VLBW infants. Only studies reporting clinical outcomes were considered. Data collection and analysis were performed in accordance with the rigorous standards set by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Three eligible trials were identified. Two of these trials, including one with a significantly larger sample size than the others combined, were conducted in regions where the population had low baseline selenium levels. A meta-analysis of the pooled data revealed that selenium supplementation significantly reduced the proportion of infants experiencing one or more episodes of sepsis. The summary relative risk (RR) was 0.73 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.57 to 0.93), with a risk difference (RD) of -0.10 (95% CI: -0.17 to -0.02). This translates to a number needed to treat (NNT) of 10 (95% CI: 5.9 to 50). However, selenium supplementation did not lead to improvements in survival rates, reductions in neonatal chronic lung disease, or decreases in the incidence of retinopathy of prematurity. The authors concluded that selenium supplementation in very preterm infants is associated with a reduction in the occurrence of sepsis. However, it does not appear to improve survival rates or reduce the risk of chronic neonatal lung disease or retinopathy of prematurity. It is suggested that higher doses of selenium than those currently recommended for infants receiving parenteral nutrition may be beneficial. It is important to note that the findings are heavily influenced by one large trial conducted in a region with low selenium levels, which may limit the generalizability of the results to populations in other geographical areas.
